Swedish Exporters Feel Pressure as U.S. Tariffs Take Toll Across Sectors

STOCKHOLM, June 13—Swedish exporters are facing mounting challenges after the United States imposed broad-based tariffs on a wide range of Swedish goods last month, a move that has sent ripples through the nation’s economy and raised concerns among policymakers and businesses alike. The tariffs, which came into effect on May 10, target Swedish exports including machinery, pharmaceuticals, timber products, and electronics, among others.

According to the Swedish Trade Federation, the new duties—averaging 20 percent—have already led to a noticeable slowdown in shipments to the U.S., Sweden’s third-largest non-EU trading partner. Early data from the National Board of Trade show that exports to the U.S. fell nearly 18 percent in May compared to the previous year.

“We are seeing immediate consequences. Swedish manufacturers are losing competitiveness in the American market, and some contracts have been suspended or renegotiated,” said Kerstin Åberg, chief economist at the federation. “The impact is broad, not limited to any single industry.”

The U.S. administration cited concerns over what it described as “persistent trade imbalances” and “unfair subsidies” in its decision to introduce the tariffs. Negotiations between Swedish and U.S. trade officials are ongoing, but a swift resolution appears unlikely.

At the port of Gothenburg, Sweden’s largest, officials report a sharp decrease in outbound container traffic bound for North America. “Volumes are down by about a fifth since the tariffs began,” said Lars Holm, commercial manager at the port. “Exporters are telling us they’re looking for alternative markets or delaying shipments.”

Local unions have warned of possible job losses if the situation persists. “Workers across sectors—from pharmaceuticals to engineering—are worried,” said Anna Lindström, spokesperson for the Swedish Industrial Workers Union. “If this continues, layoffs will be inevitable at some plants.”

The government has expressed concern, with Minister for Foreign Trade, Johan Berg, calling the tariffs “disproportionate and harmful to both sides.” He added, “We are working with our partners in the EU to address this issue collectively.”

Analysts warn that if the tariffs remain in place, Sweden’s GDP growth could be trimmed by up to 0.4 percentage points this year. For now, businesses and workers alike are bracing for further disruption as trade talks continue without resolution.
